Take it down," and very shortly, we have no press at all. From the Near v. Minnesota majority opinion:

the fact that liberty of press may be abused does not make any less necessary the immunity of the press from prior restraint.

Near v. Minnesota established that such restrictions are unconstitutional. You cannot legally stop the press from publishing anything, unless it is one of three exceptional cases:

1: If it reveals crucial military information, such as the future departure dates of ships during wartime (in NYT v US, it was deemed that "national security" is far too broad a description to meet this standard, see the concurring opinion of Justice Black in that case)

The guarding of military and diplomatic secrets at the expense of informed representative government provides no real security

2: If it contains obscenity
3: If it may directly incite acts of violence (future rulings have interpreted this as a specific call to action - as in "reader, kill this person." This interpretation specifically addresses the issue above of libel regulations being made overly broad) If it does not fall under any of those three categories, you may only punish the press from abuses, NOT prevent it from publishing. Abuses would include things like Libel (knowingly publishing inaccurate material with the intent to damage an entity's reputation). It is also noted that the responsibility of determining eligibility for prior restraint falls on the government; in other words, they must meaningfully demonstrate, to a high standard of proof, that the material is harmful, and CANNOT require an outlet demonstrate it is NOT before publishing. Punishment of a press outlet for publishing classified information that was provided to it by an unaffiliated source, rather than the outlet being itself the source has been deemed unconstitutional (Landmark Communications v Virginia).
